name: Variance Analysis
purpose: Collects and organises information on performance variances, normally for schedule, cost and quality. For each it states planned result, actual result, variance, root cause and planned response. The book calls variance analysis a data analysis technique, used in the five processes above, and says the result can stand alone, sit inside the project status report, or back up an earned value status report.

provides_to.what: the analysis can be provided as part of the project status report (prose)
the analysis can be provided as backup to an earned value status report (prose); the book names no form number, 4.4 is matched by title

alignment.what_must_agree: variances and root causes must match those in the team member reports
variances and root causes must match those in the project status report
planned and actual schedule results must match the project schedule
planned costs must agree with the cost estimates

alignment.form: Project budget (no form of this name in the book)
alignment.what_must_agree: planned and actual costs must agree with the project budget; the book has no form named project budget (not stated in the book)
variances that became issues must match the issue log
the book writes "earned value status report"; the matching form is the Earned Value Analysis Report (4.4), whose variances must agree with these
the book writes "contractor status report"; the matching form is the Contractor Status Report (4.6), whose variances must agree with these

elements.guidance: Describe the work planned to be accomplished.
Identify the root cause of the variance.
Document the planned corrective or preventive action.
Record the planned costs for the work planned to be accomplished.
Identify the root cause of the variance.
Document the planned corrective or preventive action.
Describe the planned performance or quality measurements.
Describe the actual performance or quality measurements.
Identify the root cause of the variance.
Document the planned corrective action; Table 4.3 says corrective only, not corrective or preventive, for quality.

tailoring: Scope variance can be included, but it is generally shown by the schedule variance, because more or less scope will have been done over time.
The analysis can be done at activity, resource, work package, control account or project level, as needed.
Add a check box saying whether the information must be escalated to the sponsor, program manager or other appropriate individuals.
Add a field for the implications of continued variance, such as a forecast based on trend analysis or on identified responses.
Tailor the presentation as well as the content: many PMOs have reporting software that turns the data into dashboards, heat reports, stop light charts or other representations.

decisions.decision: What the planned and actual results were and how big the variance is
decisions.notes: Repeated under Schedule Variance, Cost Variance and Quality Variance.

decisions.decision: What the planned response to each variance is
decisions.notes: Corrective or preventive for schedule and cost; corrective for quality.

decisions.decision: Whether the variance must be escalated
decisions.notes: Only a Tailoring Tip, which suggests adding a check box.

citation: Book of Forms form 4.3, PDF pages 213 to 214 (printed pages 202 to 203)
notes: Table 4.3 has three parent rows (Schedule variance, Cost variance, Quality variance), each with five sub-rows; they are listed as "Parent: sub", and the printed labels repeat three times on the blank form (PDF pages 215 to 216, printed pages 204 to 205). On the blank form the cost section spans the page break. The prose says the information can be standalone, part of 4.2, or backup to an earned value status report. The book does not say what feeds the planned and actual results beyond the Alignment list (not stated in the book), so receives_from is empty. Table 4.3 gives no formula for a variance; the cost row says only calculate the variance (not stated in the book).
